segments.text: Light can be trapped. Glass fibres carry it under oceans, and photonic chips route it through wires half a micron wide.
This ring, a few microns across, sorts colours. Send in several, and most pass straight by…
…but one colour drops into the ring, circles it, and leaves through the other wire.
How do you trap light in a wire? And why do only certain colours fit?
Start with a strip of glass, the core, surrounded by material of lower refractive index, the cladding.
A ray that meets the wall at a shallow angle can't escape. It's totally reflected, and zigzags along the core.
But light is a wave. The zigzag is really two plane waves crossing: one heading up, one heading down.
Together they form a standing wave across the core, which travels along it.
But not every angle works. Follow the wave up across the core and back: it must return in step with itself, or the bounces cancel.
So the round-trip phase must be a whole number of turns, 2πm. Slide the angle, and only a few angles click into place.
These are the modes. Each keeps its shape as it travels, with tails that fade into the cladding: evanescent waves.
There's a cleaner way to find modes, with linear algebra.
A mode is a shape E(x) that travels as e^(iβz). Put that into the wave equation, and out comes an eigenvalue problem.
Sample x on a grid. The second derivative becomes a tridiagonal matrix, and the index profile adds to its diagonal.
Its eigenvectors are the mode shapes. Its eigenvalues give each mode's propagation constant, β.
And each effective index, β/k₀, lies between the cladding and core indices.
Any input is a sum of modes, each advancing its own phase. It's the angular spectrum method from episode one, with modes in place of plane waves.
Launch an off-centre spot into a wide guide. The modes beat into a kaleidoscope, then fall back in step, and the spot reappears.
Now place two identical guides side by side, so close that their tails overlap, and launch light into one.
It drifts across into the other guide, then comes back, again and again.
Why? The pair has modes of its own: one symmetric, one antisymmetric, with propagation constants β + κ and β − κ.
Light in one guide is the sum of the two. One slowly falls behind, and after a distance π/2κ it has flipped sign: now the sum sits in the other guide.
In the basis of the two guides, that's a 2×2 rotation: amplitude cos κz in one, i sin κz in the other.
Stop halfway and you have a 50:50 splitter, the building block of interferometers, switches and optical processors.
To store light, bend a guide into a ring beside a straight one. On every pass, a little light leaks across into the ring.
Each round trip adds another copy, rotated by the round-trip phase, and a little weaker than the last.
Off resonance, the copies curl into a small spiral, and mostly cancel.
On resonance, when the ring fits a whole number of wavelengths, they line up into one long arrow. The light piles up.
Sweep the colour, and the stored light spikes at evenly spaced resonances. That's what the ring in the opening did.
How sharp is each spike? That's set by loss: the more round trips the light survives, the narrower the peak.
We measure it with the quality factor: the wavelength over the peak's width, Q = λ/Δλ. High Q means light stays stored for a long time.
Now watch the light that goes straight past. It meets the light leaking back out of the ring, which on resonance comes out flipped.
So the through port dims. When the ring leaks out exactly as fast as it loses light inside, the two cancel completely: critical coupling.
Couple more weakly, or more strongly, and the dip gets shallower.
On a computer, each idea takes just a few lines.
Modes: build the tridiagonal matrix and call an eigenvalue solver. Make the window wide enough for the tails, or its edges squeeze the modes.
Propagation: the beam propagation method, BPM. It alternates two steps: diffraction, an FFT as in episode one, and refraction, a thin phase screen.
Repeat, slice after slice. That's how the coupler was computed.
Resonators: add up the round trips, a geometric series, in one line.
The catch: BPM only marches forward, at gentle angles. Fine for couplers, but wrong for tight bends and reflections.
Trapped light settles into modes, the eigenvectors of the cross-section. A resonator stores light where round trips add in phase.
But these shortcuts assume gentle, forward-going light. Sharp bends, gratings and nanostructures break that, and then you need Maxwell's equations themselves.
How does a computer solve them? Next time.
